title: The Lesson I Learned From Absalom's Hair
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Absalom's Hair
There are some tragedies in Scripture that begin long before the moment everyone remembers.
Most people remember Absalom hanging from a tree.
Few remember how he got there.
Fewer still realize that the very thing he celebrated became the thing that destroyed him.
And if we're honest, that's not just Absalom's story.
It's ours.
Because sometimes the gifts God gives us become idols we worship.
Sometimes the blessings we receive become the source of our pride.
Sometimes the thing that makes us feel important becomes the thing that slowly pulls us away from the One who gave it.
Absalom's hair was not evil.
But what happened in his heart was.
And that changes everything.
The son who looked like a king
The Bible introduces Absalom in a way that feels almost cinematic.
"Now in all Israel there was no one who was praised as much as Absalom for his good looks. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him." (2 Samuel 14:25)
This was not ordinary attractiveness.
This was extraordinary beauty.
Absalom possessed the kind of appearance that immediately commanded attention.
People noticed him.
People admired him.
People talked about him.
He carried the presence of royalty.
And then Scripture gives us a fascinating detail.

"When he cut the hair of his head—he used to cut his hair from time to time when it became too heavy for him—he would weigh it, and its weight was two hundred shekels by the royal standard." (2 Samuel 14:26)
The biblical writer could have skipped that detail.
But God included it.
Why?
Because the Holy Spirit was showing us something important.
Absalom's hair had become part of his identity.
Part of his image.
Part of the thing that made him stand out.
Part of what made him feel powerful.
The Hebrew text repeatedly highlights his physical excellence.
The word used for praise and admiration carries the idea of public acclaim.
People celebrated him.
People admired him.
People elevated him.
And somewhere along the way, admiration became fuel.
Fuel for ambition.
Fuel for pride.
Fuel for rebellion.
The dangerous intoxication of being admired
Most people think pride begins with arrogance.
Often it begins with applause.
There is something intoxicating about being noticed.
Being admired.
Being celebrated.
Being validated.
Being told you're special.
Being told you're gifted.
Being told you're different.
The human heart was never designed to handle worship.
Only God was.
Yet many of us spend our lives chasing what only God can safely receive.
Likes.
Recognition.
Status.
Influence.
Followers.
Success.
Beauty.
Achievements.
Reputation.
None of these things are inherently sinful.
But they become dangerous when they begin feeding our identity more than God's presence does.
Absalom's problem was not his appearance.
His problem was that his appearance became bigger than his obedience.
And whenever image becomes bigger than obedience, destruction is already growing beneath the surface.
The rebellion growing in secret
The story becomes darker.
Absalom eventually begins stealing the hearts of Israel.
Notice the language carefully.
The text says:
"So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." (2 Samuel 15:6)
The Hebrew verb is גָּנַב (ganab).
It means to steal.
To take what does not belong to you.
To secretly remove something from its rightful owner.
Absalom wasn't simply gaining popularity.
He was stealing loyalty.
The loyalty that belonged to God-appointed authority.
The loyalty that belonged to the king.
The loyalty that ultimately belonged to the Lord Himself.
And here's what makes this so relevant today.
People can look spiritually successful while secretly building kingdoms for themselves.
Crowds can gather around someone while their heart drifts further from God.
Influence can increase while intimacy with God decreases.
Followers can multiply while humility disappears.
Platforms can grow while character shrinks.
Absalom mastered appearances.
But God sees beneath appearances.
God always sees beneath appearances.
The moment nobody forgets
The rebellion eventually led to war.
Father against son.
Kingdom against kingdom.
The story reaches its unforgettable climax in 2 Samuel 18.
As Absalom fled through the forest riding a mule, Scripture records a shocking moment.
"His head got caught fast in the oak, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth." (2 Samuel 18:9)
The text does not explicitly say it was his hair.
Many paintings and sermons have assumed it was.
The Hebrew text specifically mentions his head.
Yet considering the emphasis Scripture previously places upon his hair, generations of believers have recognized the profound symbolism.
Whether hair, head, or both became entangled, the lesson remains unmistakable.
The thing associated with his glory became associated with his downfall.
The thing that once elevated his image became part of the image of his defeat.
He hung helplessly between heaven and earth.
Unable to save himself.
Unable to free himself.
Unable to escape the consequences of his rebellion.
And suddenly the handsome prince looked very different.
The applause was gone.
The admiration was gone.
The image was gone.
Only reality remained.
The Gospel hidden inside the tragedy
This is where many people stop reading.
But Christians cannot stop there.
Because every story in Scripture ultimately points beyond itself.
It points to Jesus.
Absalom hung helplessly because of his rebellion.
Jesus hung willingly because of ours.
Absalom sought a throne through pride.
Jesus left a throne through humility.
Absalom stole hearts.
Jesus redeems hearts.
Absalom brought division.
Jesus brings reconciliation.
Absalom's story ends in judgment.
Jesus' story creates an invitation to grace.
The contrast is breathtaking.
The Apostle Paul writes that Christ:
The Greek word translated "humbled" is ἐταπείνωσεν (etapeinōsen).
It means to lower oneself voluntarily.
To choose humility.
To surrender status.
To embrace obedience.
Absalom grasped for exaltation.
Jesus embraced humiliation.
And because He did, sinners like us can receive mercy.
This is where the story suddenly becomes personal.
Maybe your "hair" is not literal.
Maybe it's your career.
Your intelligence.
Your influence.
Your beauty.
Your success.
Your ministry.
Your accomplishments.
Your reputation.
Your talents.
Your platform.
Your wealth.
Your education.
Your popularity.
The question is not whether these things are gifts.
The question is whether they have quietly become your identity.
Anything we place above Christ eventually becomes a burden too heavy to carry.
The very thing we depend upon apart from God eventually disappoints us.
Every idol eventually collapses under its own weight.
Only Christ can carry the weight of our souls.
The Hebrew word for glory is כָּבוֹד (kavod).
Interestingly, the root carries the idea of weight.
True glory belongs to God because only God can bear the weight of glory.
We cannot.
Absalom tried.
And it crushed him.
Jesus carries glory because He is glory.
And when we surrender to Him, we finally stop carrying burdens we were never meant to bear.
The invitation hidden in the warning
Absalom's story is not merely a warning.
It is an invitation.
An invitation to examine our hearts.
An invitation to surrender our pride.
An invitation to stop building our own kingdoms.
An invitation to trust the King who gave His life for rebels.
Perhaps the most dangerous idols are not the sinful things.
Perhaps they are the good things that quietly replace God.
The gifts that become gods.
The blessings that become masters.
The successes that become saviors.
Absalom teaches us that what we worship eventually controls us.
Jesus teaches us that who we worship transforms us.
That difference changes everything.
Maybe while reading this, the Holy Spirit brought something specific to mind.
Something you've been holding too tightly.
Something you've been finding identity in.
Something that has become more important than obedience.
Don't ignore that conviction.
God's grace often begins where our excuses end.
And if this article exposed something hidden, be honest.
Your honesty may become the testimony someone else desperately needed to see.
Some people are hanging from things they still think are helping them.
Others are exhausted from carrying crowns they were never meant to wear.
The human heart forgets quickly.
The Gospel reminds us constantly.
Every article, study, resource, and discipleship tool exists to help people know Jesus more deeply and make Him known more boldly.
Not for attention. Not for algorithms. But because someone scrolling today may be one moment away from remembering that God's grace is greater than their failure.
Because the greatest lesson from Absalom's hair is not how pride destroys people.
It is how Christ saves proud people who finally surrender.
The crown you keep protecting may be the very thing keeping you from the King.
